senses: To move materials with a shovel.
To move with a shoveling motion, to cover as by shoveling
To shuffle or shamble.
To go about begging.
ety: From Middle English schovele (> English dialectal shoul, shool), from Old English sċofl (“shovel”), from Proto-Germanic *skuflō, *skūflō (“shovel”), equivalent to shove + -el (instrumental/agent suffix). Cognate with Scots shuffle, shule, shuil (“shovel”), Saterland Frisian Sköifel (“shovel”), West Frisian skoffel, schoffel (“hoe, spade, shovel”), Dutch schoffel (“spade, hoe”), Low German Schüfel, Schuffel (“shovel”), German Schaufel (“shovel”), Danish skovl (“shovel”), Swedish skyffel, skovel (“shovel”), Icelandic skófla (“shovel”).
examples: The workers were shooling gravel and tarmac into the pothole in the road.

senses: A grandfather, especially one with Italian ancestry.
The branch of engineering and technology that is concerned with the construction of devices that use the flow and pressure of a fluid in circuits analogous to electronic ones
Components generally.
An inner room or nuptial chamber.
ety: Borrowed from Latin thalamus, from Ancient Greek θάλαμος (thálamos, “an inner chamber, a bedroom, a bed”).

senses: Synonym of hemorrhoid.
Situated between the Earth and the Moon.
Situated below the orbit of the Moon, or equivalent distance from the Earth.
examples: The economic viability of commercial operations in cislunar space – meaning the region extending from Earth’s atmosphere to the lunar surface and beyond – might be even more remote.

senses: Resembling or pertaining to hair, especially in slenderness or fineness.
ety: From Latin capillāris (“pertaining to the hair”), from capillus (“the hair, properly of the head”), from caput (“head”).

senses: Flesh-eating; (usually also specifically) predatorily so: that is, predatory.
The currency of the former Czechoslovakia, divided into 100 hellers.
The currency of the Czech Republic, divided into 100 hellers.
The former currency of Slovakia, divided into 100 haliers.
ety: From Czech and Slovak koruna; cognate with krone and German Krone. Doublet of corona, crown, korona, krona, króna, and krone.

senses: A man who delivers bread.
Having a single tube.
The property of being regional.
examples: The party's regionality prevented it from winning a national election.

senses: The act of affirming, affirmation
ety: Either affirm + -ance or from Old French afermance

senses: Any timber prop to support a structure.
ety: Related to German Stollen (“stull”), ultimately from Proto-Germanic *stullô (“support, post, beam”), but its route into English is uncertain. Perhaps borrowed from Middle High German stolle. Doublet of stollen. Compare also stum.

senses: A man who uses a knife as a weapon.
A type of flat-top grill used for cooking, composed of a thick plate of metal above the heating element to provide thermal mass and eliminate hot spots.
ety: From Spanish plancha. Doublet of phalanx, phalange, planch, planche, and plank.

senses: A kind of coarse parchment for book covers; a forrill.
ety: From Middle English forel (“case, sheath”), from Old French forrel, fourrel.

senses: Someone who zones things.
Without any successful songs.
Completed without taking damage (getting hit).
examples: While she was hitless herself, Denise produced R & B hits like Bill Coday's "Get Your Lie Straight" and the Sequins' "Hey Romeo."
You get an achievement for pulling off a hitless first area.

senses: A person, especially a soldier, who is on guard; especially, a masculine one.
A member of the National Guard; especially, a masculine one.
A member of a Guards regiment; especially, a masculine one.
One yen (unit of Japanese currency); a coin worth one yen.
ety: From yen + -y (diminutive suffix), probably influenced by penny.

senses: The evergreen shrub Juniperus sabina, endemic to Europe, which yields a medicinal oil.
The poisonous dried tips of this plant, with anthelmintic properties, used as a drug.
The eastern red cedar, Juniperus virginiana, of eastern North America.
ety: Inherited from Middle English savyne, from Old French savine, from Latin sabīna. Compare Old English safine.

senses: One who has renounced.
ety: From Latin renuntiātus, past participle of Latin renūntiāre. Doublet of renounce.

senses: That cants or preaches in a false manner.
A mass, usually of hair or undigested vegetable matter, found in a human or animal's intestines, similar to a hairball.
An enterolith.
ety: Borrowed from Spanish bezoar and/or French bézoard, based on Arabic بَازَهْر (bāzahr), from Middle Persian pʾtzhl (pādzahr, “bezoar, antidote”), from a compound of words meaning “to protect” and “poison” (literally “killing thing”), thus a bezoar was “that which protects against poison”. In ancient times, bezoars from animals were ground up and ingested as remedies for various maladies and as antidotes to poisons.

senses: A network of geocells sometimes forming a geospacer
A type of Italian herbal liqueur.
examples: At Vessel, in Seattle, the bar manager, Jamie Boudreau, starts his cherry bitters by combining separate bourbon- and rye-based infusions with a touch of honey-flavored vodka and the Italian digestif amaro.
In addition, there's a full bar, with some excellent specialty cocktails and a good list of grappa, amari and dessert wines.

There are two dozen cocktails and shots, from whiskey punches to tiki-style drinks. (The three-rum old-fashioned should be a summertime classic.) There's a hearty focus on the bitter Italian aperitifs known as amaros.

senses: A fish, the cavally or jurel.
A fish, the pompano (Trachinotus carolinus).
ety: Probably of same origin as cavally.

senses: Any of a number of tiny fish in the Cyprinodontiformes order of ray-finned fish.
ety: From killie (“killifish”, perhaps from kill (“channel, creek”)) or kill, + fish.

senses: A mausoleum or shrine in the Arab world.
An ironworker.
ety: From Middle English blomer, from blome (“iron ingot”) (modern English bloom), from Old English blōma.

senses: A grape variety from Puglia, genetically identical to zinfandel; the red wine made from this grape.
ety: Borrowed from Italian primitivo. Doublet of primitive.

senses: A painful condition caused by irritation of cartilage, often in the undersurface of the kneecap.
A subset thus obtained.
An aspect of planets that are distant from each other by one fifth of a zodiac (72°)
examples: Effectively no household making less than $28,000 will pay federal income tax – usually about 15% of the bottom income quintile has some tax liability.

senses: The concept of hospitality to strangers.
ety: Borrowed from New Latin xenia, from Ancient Greek ξενῐ́ᾱ (xenĭ́ā, “hospitality”).

senses: Having lobes.
Someone or something that burrows.
An animal that lives in an underground hole that it has made itself.
A bicycle capable of levitation.
examples: Ethics does not compel you to make it a family heirloom, passing it down from generation to generation, into the distant future, when the cool kids are riding those antigravity skycycles.

senses: That which dilutes.
A solvent or other liquid preparation used to dilute a sample prior to testing.
ety: Latin diluens, from diluere. See dilute.
